item.title: The grid is a promise, not a cage
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Every layout begins with a small act of faith: that someone will give us ninety seconds of their attention. A grid is how we keep that promise.

Start with the reading order

Before we draw a single column, we write the page as a list: headline, standfirst, image, caption, proof, action. If the list does not make sense read aloud, no grid will rescue it.

A grid is not a cage. It is a promise that the reader will always know where to look next.

Break it on purpose

Rules earn their keep when they are broken with reason. We let a headline cross two gutters when it is the only idea on the page. The break should read as emphasis, not accident.

  • One idea per section.
  • Three widths, no more.
  • Test with the longest headline.

The test is simple. Cover the design and ask whether the reading order still holds.
item.excerpt:encoded: A grid is not a cage for ideas. It is a promise that the reader will always know where to look next.

item.title: Type at the edge of legibility
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Type has two lives. One is to be looked at; the other is to be read. Most of our arguments in the studio are about which life a particular line is living.

Reading is a physical act

At 16px, a reader's eye lands four to seven times per line. Too wide, and the return sweep gets lost. Too tight, and the line breaks in the middle of an idea.

Legibility is not the opposite of personality. It is the condition that lets personality be trusted.

Set the small things well

Footnotes, captions, and form labels are where typography tells the truth. A studio that sets a beautiful cover but a careless error message has shown you its priorities.

Good type does not announce itself. It simply makes the next sentence easier to start.
item.excerpt:encoded: The best typography is not the loudest. It is the one that disappears at exactly the right moment.

item.title: Colour with a job to do
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Most colour conversations start with a reference: a photograph, a fabric, a sunset. Ours start with a list of jobs.

Four jobs, four decisions

Colour has to signal action, separate regions, soften a hard edge, and sometimes stop a reader completely. Those are different jobs, and they rarely want the same hue.

A palette becomes a system when you can name what each colour is for, not when you can name what it is.

Budget your saturation

One saturated colour per view is usually enough. The mistake is letting every tag, badge, and illustration compete. Most of the time, black and paper do the work.

Colour should feel inevitable after the fact, not impressive during the pitch.
item.excerpt:encoded: A palette is not a mood board. It is a set of jobs — signal, separate, soften, stop.

item.title: Neobrutalism grew up
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Every few years the internet rediscovers hard borders and flat colour. The first wave is always a parody. Then the style settles down and becomes useful.

What the style is actually good at

Neobrutalism makes hierarchy physical. A border says this is a thing. A shadow says this thing sits above that thing. A flat colour says this block has one job.

Brutalism without editing is just noise with a drop shadow. The minimalism is what makes the loud parts land.

The mature version

The mature version is not a mood. It is a set of commitments: readable contrast, honest surfaces, visible hierarchy, and no fake depth.

Trends are useful when they give you a vocabulary for a decision you already wanted to make. The rest is costume.
item.excerpt:encoded: Hard borders and flat colour are not a costume. Used with restraint, they make hierarchy unmistakable.
